title: Making Snake Rag: rehearsing, balance and no drums on early records
summary: Armstrong explains the band rehearsed on the job, records were cut quickly, lead was lost, drums were avoided, and he improvised breaks to Oliver's cues.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Second, yeah. Second cornet at the time. Yeah.
We both was using cornets, you know. Well now when you went in to make a record day like Snake Rag, had you been playing this tune? Had he been, had he been? Not this one. Yeah.

It's one of them he made up for the Ginette record. When he started making records then he started being a writer. Yeah. And that stuff would come up later, you know. Would you rehearse that then in the studio before you recorded it? Well we'd rehearse that on the job, you know. Uh-huh. And then by the time we'd get to the studio all they'd do is cut it up and time it to, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. For no trouble at all, you know, to make them records, because they'd make one after another. It wasn't as particular as it was today, you know. Well you don't think you made mistakes in there, do you? Well, in fact, but we could have had more lead. Uh-huh. See, we could have pushed Joe up or stand him out or we could have played a little softer or we could have... For the balance on it. So that lead. Yeah. That's where, in all of them old records you lose that lead. Uh-huh. See what I mean? You notice, when everybody got the blood then, the lead was gone.
Now you spoke before about how they didn't have the drums. Baby Dodds just played Woodblocks. Uh, that daughter's baby was there.

Yeah. Yeah. They didn't need him nowhere. They didn't use drums at all, right? No drums at all at that time. They were scared it would throw the needle off. I see. Yeah. So we got back good. But the only thing I have about those early recordings is that you didn't get that lead much. That's what I mean, because you couldn't do, you couldn't tell Joe what to do. Yeah. He was the boss. Yeah. Now those breaks that you two took on there. Well, yeah. Well, I put notes to his lead, whatever he made. I just, we didn't write it. Did you rehearse it? No. Just for the woman. He'd tell me why the band was playing. What are you going to play on the line? What is this? I'd figure out my notes. He'd give you cues. That's why all the musicians used to come around to hear us do that, you know. They'd have a little secret we had. You know, everybody cool on that. Yeah, Nick's and Lufa-Nickel, Paul Whitewood and all the boys used to come around, you know. And they thought that was something. And he would change the things he was going to do from night to night until... Yeah, whatever he was going to do. He let me know about four or five balls a while the band was jumping, you know.
